lines.text: Welcome to DVDASA with David Choe and Asa Akira, with special guest Joe Rogan, and very, very special guest Yoshi Obayashi. [mock-formal] That's a very professional introduction. You guys are legit. We found that he's the best at it. You guys are making it happen. He's the star of the show. So there you go, you heard it — correct.

Joe Rogan is here. Joe was nice enough to have me and Yoshi on his podcast. Very nice. It was my honor. You guys were awesome, it was so fun. You're like the podcast king. Yeah, that's the thing — you're the podcast master. I knew a little bit, but I didn't know you were, like, the fucking podcast man.

And then it's like, you've got millions of downloads and listeners, and your fans are fucking crazy. [correcting himself] They're very nice people. They're like Death Squad Australia, Death Squad Japan.
It's a little crazy at this point. That's cool to have that kind of... Do you like your fans? Yeah, they're very nice people. Or do you hate them? No, no, no. I don't hate them at all.
I wait after my shows. I take pictures with people. I'll stay for hours. I'll do an hour and ten on stage and then spend at least twice that taking pictures. Wow.

I saw that at the Ice House — every one of them, you stay until... Yeah, I try to. The only time I can't is when they turn a room over. Like if I'm working at an Improv and they have a seven and a nine, when you're done they only have 20 minutes

to clear the room and bring in the new crowd. So it takes a long time, and if you're blocking the place with lines to take pictures, it could take an hour and a half. So let me ask you about that, since we have a young, burgeoning comedian — powerful Yoshi.
I've known Yoshi forever. I would hardly say he's burgeoning — he's hilarious. No, I know. Yoshi is an old veteran in the comedy world. So how did you get into that? How did you start doing it?
I just started doing open mic nights. I just did an open mic night. Like after you were already successful? No, no, no. That's what I did first. That's what you did before anything.
But you were fighting first, right? Yeah, yeah. When I was still teaching martial arts and still competing, I had three kickboxing fights while I was still doing comedy. So how old were you then?

Twenty-one. So you're 21 and you're the funny guy out of your friends? No, no. That was what was fucked up. It's like, [mock encouraging] 'You're funny, Joe, you should go do an open mic night, you should...'
No, no, no, not at all. It takes a lot of balls. Because I have friends — I hang out with Yoshi and other comedians now — the funny guys I know, I'm like, hey, you should go to an open mic.

And it's so scary to have never done that. Well, I felt like I had already fought a bunch of times. You're literally fighting people. I shouldn't be scared about getting on stage. Taekwondo tournaments are full contact, and there were brutal knockouts. I escaped — I never got knocked out brutally — but I saw my friends get head-kicked and shit.

Physical pain is one thing, but the pain of the heart... yeah. I think comedy is like — to get booed off stage... you're talking crazy, it's way worse getting kicked in the head. It's way worse. So I'm like, physically I've been fucked up, I've been in the ring, so why should I be scared to get maybe booed
or made fun of on stage? The last fight I had, I got TKO'd. I got dropped with a left hook. I got up. It was three fights in a day. I was at a kickboxing tournament in Rhode Island.
It's for no money. I'm not getting any money. I was exhausted. I fought the first guy, won that fight. Won the second fight. Then I had to sit around for an hour and a half before the finals.

I was just so exhausted. This guy cracked me. Bang! So that was the last time I'd done anything dangerous in competition. So from that to going on stage, it wasn't that hard. What do you think was your favorite gig so far? You've done so much.

The podcast is my favorite. Are you just saying that because it's what you're doing now? No, no, no, it's my favorite. It's fun. But before we get into that, I just want to say — so you're fighting and you're like, I don't give a fuck about getting my ass kicked. So what was the...

Were you funny to your friends, or was it a personal thing, like, I think I'm funny and I want to try this? Well, if you went back to my high school and asked — people have asked my friends who knew me in high school — no one thought

I was funny. No one. I was not funny. I was crazy. So it was a personal challenge? Yeah, you're like, I think I'm funny? No. It came by way of guys I used to do Taekwondo with. I would make them laugh in the locker room, because before sparring, or on our

way to matches — we traveled a lot for tournaments, I'd fight almost every weekend — we fought a lot. Especially coming up, you fight in local karate tournaments, then there'd be a Taekwondo tournament. The best way to

get loose, where you feel comfortable competing, is you've got to do it a lot. If you don't do it a lot, you won't catch that groove. And when you take time off, it's really nerve-wracking. Coming back is hard, all your timing is off. That's why they call it ring rust.

It's not that you're out of shape, it's just you're not used to the danger of the experience. So I was always the guy who'd make everybody laugh in that situation — but everything I'd say was fucked up. I'd just say

the most fucked-up shit. Like this guy? Yeah, well, sort of. It was a little more — I was young, like 20, probably not as eloquent as Yoshi. It's stupid, but I'd do impressions of people we knew, and it was always someone winding up fucking somebody in

my impression. You know, [mock voice] 'this guy, and him and his friend...' I don't know, I'd come up with one of our friends, joking around. But I wasn't trying to be a comedian. These guys would laugh, and I wanted attention, so whatever would work.

I'd figure out what would make you laugh, and I'd figure out how to do it. So from that you're like, fuck it, I'm gonna give this a shot? I just used to talk about my friends. It was never anything I considered. And then did you bomb at first? Yeah, yeah, it was terrible.
Really? It was fucking awesome. But you wanted to do it again? Yeah, yeah, yeah. That humiliation — it's very addicting, isn't it? Well, I was really bad the first time, no doubt about it.

That's usually enough to make people quit. I got a couple of [weak chuckle] 'ha ha, ha ha.' Nobody really thought I was good, and I knew I wasn't good. But I saw a few people that night who were good. And I saw different levels — like Richard Jeni, one of my all-time favorite comedians, said one thing that was really cool.
He said shitty comics are great because they inspire other people to give it a chance. Oh, so you were like, I'm shitty, I'm gonna keep putting myself up there to give guys like Richard Jeni...
No, no, no, the opposite. Guys were worse than me. As shitty as I was, I saw guys with no hope. But I also saw guys who were a gradient better than an open-miker.
Someone who was just starting to get an act together. And then the same night — it was an open mic night in Boston — the emcee was Jonathan Katz.

Remember that show Dr. Katz on Comedy Central? He was the emcee the first time I ever went on stage. He was one of the local headliners. So I got to see him — really tight, really well-written jokes, a really good comic.
Great timing, very, very funny, witty guy. So I got to see him on my first night. He's like a real pro. And then I got to see some local guys.
And I was hooked. I was like, I see what's going on here. You just have to figure out how to do that. Even though I knew I didn't know how initially, I was like, there's something in here.
But that's amazing, because most people who get the itch to do something like that and then not get booed, but just... I've been to a show where Yoshi got booed before,
and I'm like, whoa. How would you ever get the balls to go back on stage? It's hard. For me... You have to want it so bad. Like you're talking about the physical stuff —
I've been in fights, I've gotten the shit kicked out of me. For me, I'm more sensitive. Yeah. To have people boo you...
I don't think I would. You mean public humiliation? To go up and say, these are jokes that make me and my friends laugh, and then they're like, get off stage.
I believe anything difficult makes you better. It makes you better at life. Well, that's why you're a champ. So you did it that one time and thought, this is what I'm going to do now.
I'm not going to fight anymore, I'm going to be a comedian. Pretty much, yeah, it was almost immediate. Within maybe three to six months I quit everything.
I was teaching at Boston University. I had my own school. I had this wing attached to a Nautilus Plus gym in Revere, and I ran my own school there for a while.
And I just said, I can't do both, because I'm not concentrating on either one the right way. I like to get obsessed with things. I like to find something — especially back then.
I'm much more diverse now, much more patient now. But when I was 21, I'd lock onto something and be a maniac. I'd practice it 10 hours a day until I fell asleep.

That's just how I was when I was young. So I knew I wasn't doing myself a service spreading myself into two worlds. And the competition world was starting to freak me out, because I saw so many people get hurt.
I saw so many of my friends get fucking kicked in the head. Was that your original dream, though — to be a UFC kind of champion? No, no.

There was no UFC back then. I wanted to win the Olympics for Taekwondo. Whoa. Yeah. The problem was... Do you like kimchi? Love kimchi. So you like all... Korean, yeah. Why would you pick Taekwondo out of all...

Well, that's how I started, in a Taekwondo school. But why did you pick that instead of karate or kung fu? Back then nobody really knew. I started martial arts in 1980, probably '80 or '81, somewhere around there.

How did you get in — because Boston's a tough town? Yeah, I was little. I hated being picked on, and I moved to a new high school at 14, and there were so many kids fucking with me. I'm like, I can't do this anymore. Alright, bitches — I've got to find a martial arts school

and cut this off, whatever this is. It's a terrible feeling as a young guy not knowing how to defend yourself. But let me get this right — in the 1980s I'd think Taekwondo was the most unsexy... Karate Kid was coming out, so why wouldn't you take kung fu? Well, I started out taking karate. I took one karate class

at this place, but it was really far for me to get to. I didn't have a car, I was only 14. It was a real pain in the ass to get to, so I only went there once. And then I was coming home from a Red Sox game — it was just total luck.
And I knew there was this Taekwondo school — Jay Kim's Taekwondo Institute. I always knew about the place because they had a big ad in the Yellow Pages. Back then a full-page ad was the shit.
There was no internet. But if you turned to the Yellow Pages under martial arts, I'm like, damn, look how big this ad is. It was a dude throwing a flying sidekick in the air.
That was Jay Kim. And it showed all his credentials. Was it a big school? Yeah, yeah, very big. I was super lucky I walked into it, because it was one of the best martial arts schools in the country.

Cool guy. Amazing guy. Yeah, amazing. So even just opening a Yellow Pages to find a karate school is like a whole Karate Kid situation. Sort of. So you get to a new high school, which is always rough. It wasn't too bad. Nobody

actually beat me up, but there were always threats. I didn't have any friends, I didn't know anybody. Did somebody get douchey with you and you didn't like it? Were you a weird kid? No, no, I wasn't too weird. I mean, we're all weird when

we're 14, but it was just because I was the new guy. You had no friends? No, I just moved from another part of town. Luckily the part of Boston I moved from was a way worse neighborhood, so I was used to scary, dangerous kids. When I lived in Boston I lived in Jamaica

Plain, which was a really low-income place. It was dangerous — our house was broken into, our car was broken into. It was real sketchy. I'd go to school there — I was in seventh grade, and there was a kid in my class who was 17.

No bullshit, he was 17. For two years we lived in a really low-income, scary part of Boston. It was fucking dangerous, man. Were you a real skinny kid? Yeah, I was tiny. I wasn't very big. And who's picking on you — black kids, white kids?

Well, mostly they'd talk shit and I'd get out of the way. I wasn't into testing my manhood. I knew I didn't know how. But it was other white kids doing this sometimes? Yeah, sometimes white kids, sometimes black kids. You just didn't

want to get fucked with. I hated that feeling of not knowing what to do. And you're small. Yeah. When you don't have any friends — hey man, this motherfucker, what do I do, let's go talk to him — you don't have

any friends, you're on your own. So two or three guys get together and they don't like you, because of course I was adorable back then. [deadpan] I was cute. I had silky skin, a full head of hair. I was a bad motherfucker.

How long did it take before you could protect yourself? Who knows? I never really got to find out anything really dangerous except actual martial arts competition itself. The danger from a real person — that all went away.
You never fought the bully at your school? I hit one kid once, but I only hit him once. Knocked him out? Well, I hit him in the body. But it was avoidable.

Even looking back now — after you did the Taekwondo — I feel like I could have been nicer. Well, that's very nice of you. I just felt bad. Because back then I went from being a guy nervous about confrontation to a guy who was competing.

And competition was so scary, because you saw people get hit. You saw people get laid out, and the only reason you haven't is because no one's hit you yet. That's all it is. You're literally the perfect person to host that Fear Factor show, because all this stuff most people never do —
become a comedian, fight competitively — is the scariest shit ever, and to face your fears like that is pretty amazing.

Yeah. I think the physical contact, the actual trauma, is the scariest part. And that's what was really bothering me as I got older — I knew people I was watching suffer from the effects of getting hit in the head too many times.

When you see a guy who's punch-drunk and you say, oh, the guy fought professionally eight times, you think about those fights. But what you don't think about is all the training for those fights. That's when you get real brain damage, because there are gym wars that are some of the worst fights.

The hardest fights I've ever seen have been gym wars, where it doesn't even count on your record, but you and another guy are beating the fuck out of each other in the gym. It happens all the time. One guy hits a guy a little too hard, and the other guy

gets pissed off, and next thing you know they're fucking going at it — basically a full-blown fight — and they might have that two, three times a week. So when you do that on a regular basis, it's only a matter of time. It's like you only have a certain amount of holes

in your ticket. So that was really scary to me too, especially as I got older, I was worried about getting injured. But this is the world you come from. Just from hanging out with Yoshi and going to his comedy shows, it seems

comedians find a lot of joy when other comedians fail — they're real dark people, and that's unfortunate. But the worlds you travel in, the UFC world, the fighting world, it's filled with so much macho testosterone, competitive, this gym-war stuff you're talking about —

what happens to people who try to come in and intimidate you or muscle you? That doesn't really happen. People are almost always friendly. Well now, but back then — did you ever have to fuck people up? No, I really didn't.

After a while... You have a very distinct stoner laugh, I noticed. When did you get into weed? Because you have the stoner laugh — when you hear it, you're like, that guy smokes a lot of weed. But then you do

so much shit, you're the opposite of a stoner. Well, that's just the stoner mentality. The idea of a stoner, the generalization, has all been perpetrated by Dr. Drew. The idea is if you laugh like that... I've heard on Loveline, someone will laugh and he'll say, [Dr. Drew voice] 'well, that is a

syndrome associated with marijuana consumption.' Yeah, but... You don't believe that? It's nonsense, doesn't mean anything. It's just a silly high laugh, that's it. You're saying you had that laugh before? No, no, I'm not saying I did, but it doesn't mean there's something wrong. The idea that there's something wrong because you have a stoner laugh —

so dumb. So when did the love affair with weed start? Well, I want to address your earlier question — weed does not make you lazy. You're either lazy or you're not. I'm more ambitious because of weed, because weed makes me sensitive. And when I get
sensitive, I think about what I'm doing wrong. And when I think about what I'm doing wrong, I think about what would make me happy, what I'd have to do to give myself a sense of accomplishment.
But do you think it's like — you have 10 times the energy of a normal person, so you get frantic and obsessed with one thing, you have all this energy — and when you do the weed it just sort of...

it doesn't slow you down, but it relaxes you to a point where you can focus more. Maybe. You're the only person I've ever heard say that. We were just talking about how if you were stoned and fought, it'd be, you know, not to your advantage,
it'd make you move slower. I'd definitely fight high. You'd love that? Oh yeah, I'd love it. Because I'd be in the ring with an old friend.

I feel like if you're going to be a stoner as a full-grown adult, you better think that way, or else you'll never get shit done. What are you trying to do with it? What are you trying to accomplish? Some people are looking for an escape.
I'm looking for the opposite of an escape. I'm looking to look deeper at everything. Engage more. Yeah, I try to do a lot of perspective-changing things, whether it's go to a different place.
But I do it consciously. And then I do a lot of isolation tank stuff, because I have a tank in my house. Can I try that out? Fuck it. What's an isolation tank?
It's a tank — you guys need one here, you have a big spot. I took my friend to your friend's place. Cruise? Is that — Crash. Crash in Santa Monica. Yeah.
I took him there. Wait, what is it? Is it a weed thing? No, no, no. It's totally natural. It's a tank filled with water that you float in. And what does it do?
Well, the water is the same temperature as the surface of your skin, and there's about a thousand pounds of Epsom salts in it, so you float because of all the salt.

And since the water is the same temperature as your skin, once you settle in and relax, you don't feel the water anymore. You don't feel anything. You're floating. You feel no difference between the air and the water.

And then you close the tank. You're totally floating. The door's shut, so you're in total darkness — complete darkness, total silence. It's what's called sensory deprivation. There's no true sensory deprivation, so they like to call it isolation.
It's an isolation thing. It feels like you're floating in space. Exactly. Well, you can't see... You can't see, hear — that's sensory deprivation. You can't do anything. It's nothing.
You don't feel anything, you don't see anything, you don't hear anything. It's about as close to a total absence of sensory input as you can get. So it's like a meditation thing?
It's way better than that. When do you start jerking off — right after? [deadpan] Right away. Right away, I don't even waste time. Get it out of the way first. You walk in jerking off.
I do jerk off before I go in, to go in with a clear mind. Nice. And how long do you stay in there? Two hours, usually about two hours. Really? And what do you do?
You just think? Yeah, just think, just lie there. That sounds awesome. Well, the world is a fucking distracting place. Do you do this every day? Not every day, no.
Just whenever I want to. Like how often? It's in my house, I don't know. Oh wow. It's in my basement. Great mentally, but does it have any physical benefits? Yes, it's great for you.
It's relaxing physically too. It's one of the best sources of magnesium. When did you get into this?

I think 2003. Like Michael Jackson told you about it? No, no, no. Altered States. You ever see the movie Altered States? Yeah, that's what it's about. And you're like, fuck it, I'm gonna get one of those?

Yeah. Well, there was a guy named John Lilly, a psychedelic pioneer. He's the guy who invented the isolation tank. I met him. You met him? When I graduated high school in 1988, my friend's mom bought tickets for all these speakers near LAX.

I didn't know who he was. And there was also another guy who gave acid to a dolphin — he was there too. Well, he's a pioneer in interspecies communication. Lilly learned a lot about communicating with dolphins from a tank.
He'd set up a tank right next to the dolphin tank, go in there and drop acid, and he said he was communicating with the dolphins. I think that's kind of evil, to give acid to dolphins.
No, no, no. Lilly would take the acid himself, and then go in with the dolphins. He was in the isolation tank right next to them. Can you get me one of these isolation tanks?
Dude, I'll hook you up. I'll have Crash come and install one. Wait, this guy's name is Crash? Yeah, his name is Crash. That sounds amazing. His real name is Craig. Well, it is amazing.

You could use it too. The people I know who run tank centers say that for years no one was talking about it — they were losing business. I couldn't believe it, because I'm like, this is something people need to know about. How am I the only one who knows about this? Wait, are you thinking about nothing?

That's dangerous. Oh, fuck yeah. Or you're thinking about nothing. You think about whatever you want. You can go in with an idea — sometimes I'll go in with a bit I'm working on, on purpose, and say, alright, I'm gonna figure this bit out.

I'll lie down and start exploring all the different possibilities in my mind. But like I was saying about the world being distracting — Sounds claustrophobic. It's not, it's the opposite. Everything's distracting, man.

Sitting in a seat is distracting. Your legs are sending a message to your brain that there's a chair underneath you. The fact that we're all in this room. The fact that he's behind me checking his Facebook.
You know what I'm saying? All of this is distracting. We're all aware of our environments and the space between us. So it's something you're calculating all the time. I would freak out.
I feel like I'd be scared to. No, no, no. I'd freak out because I'd want to write stuff down. Well, it's okay — you can set up a recorder that works on voice activation.
No way. Yeah, yeah. So when you're in there you just start talking: [whispering] 'check, check, here we go, I just had an idea,' and it'll be recording you. So what was this created for initially?
That's what I was getting to. John Lilly, the psychedelic pioneer, created it because he was trying to figure out a way to isolate the senses from the mind — to silence all the stuff around the mind.
Because anything you're doing is hard to do when there are distractions. If you're working on computer code and right next to you there's a guy with a jackhammer, it's going to be really hard.
Because you're battling this input. We don't think about the fact that there's only one way to eliminate input completely. You've got to shut off all the senses. Well, how do you do that?
You can't do it lying in a bed, because you still feel the bed. There's only one way — the tank. The tank's the only environment like that on Earth.
I'm so sold. And somehow people aren't aware of this. It should be in everyone's house. It should be in schools. Well, it's probably expensive, right? Yes, it is. But it doesn't have to be.
It's not that complicated. The ones the Float Lab, where Crash works, sells are the best in the world — super high-tech. But you should be able to make one yourself.

It seems like people can make one themselves. We could go in a closet. It's not milled in a rocket ship. You need heaters — it won't be as good as the ones Float Lab sells, but the more people that have these things, the more the high end grows.

Fuck you, why play games? Because this is the shit I think about all the time. The social anxiety, the world we live in now — you can't turn it off, with the Facebook and the Twitter, especially if you have a lot of responsibilities. So
the closest I've ever gotten to isolation was being in prison, where you don't have internet, you don't have a phone. And I was in solitary confinement, so I didn't get to talk to people.
I didn't even talk for days, where I didn't even hear my own voice. But even if you could — you could speak Japanese, right? Yeah, well, the point is it just was...

No human contact. It sucks, because you're in prison and you don't have a choice. But afterward, when I got out, I thought: if I had the choice to do that — self-imposed prison — it was the most creative time I've ever had in my life. I wrote the outline for a sci-fi novel, and the outline was 2,000 pages, and I

drew hundreds and thousands of drawings, because there's nothing to do. And I can't do that now. Tonight, after the podcast, I'll sit around and go, who should I fuck tonight? [laughing] How dare you. And especially — I thought moving back to LA would be less distracting than New York. It's even worse. Why would you

think LA would be less distracting? I just figured New York's fucking crazy, this and that. But LA's way crazier than New York, really. I think so. But it's like — I have the money to buy an isolation tank, I have the money to disappear for a month every year. So this is...
Well, I'm going to get one. You need one. The other thing I'm starting to do next year: I'm going to disappear for a month or two where I don't bring the phone,

I don't bring the computer. Are you starting to feel overloaded? Completely. I can't focus. Wednesdays is when new comic books come out, and I'm a big comic guy. I'd go buy a bunch of comics and come home and read them.

What's wrong? What are you not liking about your life right now? Too much choice. Too much choice. What do you mean — everything from what to eat for dinner to who to fuck tonight? It's too many options. You have a problem of abundance, is that what you're saying? [laughing] Exactly. That's hilarious.
That's some first-world problem. It is bullshit, there it is. First one percent. That's what I'm saying, it is. But that's nothing — you're going to be unsatisfied if you do that.
I know you're enjoying it now, and it's cool for a little while, but if you feel like your work suffers... The work is definitely suffering. Well, that's going to haunt you, because the work —
It is haunting me. It should, because that's what got you there in the first place. That's your machine. That's what gets you to the dance. That's what makes you feel like who you are.
But I can do that when I shut myself off from stuff. Just got to be gangster about it, dude. Be gangster about it in your own head. Set up parameters, set up rules.

Write things down. I write things down on paper, and if I don't get everything finished, then I'm a fucking loser. And I don't like feeling like a loser, so I get things done. When I write things down, I get things done so much more. I feel like

if I put it down in physical form... I totally agree with that. Do you? Everything you're saying right now is how I used to do shit, but I was younger. You have the eye of the tiger still. There's no eye of the tiger. It is the eye of the tiger,
but it's a misrepresentation, because I'm not hungry — I just am enjoying all these things I'm doing. It's not like, oh, I've gotta fucking do this, I gotta go, I gotta go for it.
This is my time. That's all crazy. For example, the podcast doesn't make me any money. In a way, we only do it once a week, so it's the least of my things.
But I enjoy doing it. I get obsessed with it, I start thinking about it. And for you — and this is actually in context with Yoshi, because Yoshi does a fucking sick, not-for-children show,

and he can't — I've heard he's worked clean, I've never seen it personally — but do you ever change your act for anybody? No, no. That's the beautiful thing about doing stand-up and the beautiful thing about doing a podcast: I don't have a boss in those departments. I've been offered —
you go do a seven-minute set on television, but those are bullshit. Same with Yoshi — the guys on the Leno show have said if you come up with a clean act they'll put you on. I admire guys who do it.
It's fun to watch. I like — Norton puts together a good set. It's totally an art form in and of itself. But I just have no desire. I don't want to do that.
But I think times have changed too, because doing their show really doesn't matter as much as 25, 30 years ago. No, podcasts matter now more than almost anything. That's what I'm saying.

You're the rare person who's worked in network — you've worked on major network shows and had to play the game — but now you have your own podcast, your own media empire, where millions of people listen. So what's it like to work in both worlds?

Well, it's way easier this way, because you don't have to think about it. Today Tom Segura was on — Tom's a hilarious comedian. It's so easy. How do you pick your guests? I just pick them. I have a publicist I have contact people, like

authors — I've got this theoretical physicist, Dr. Amit Goswami, on this Friday. I got him through a publicist. I said, hey, go track that guy down. Do you have a wish list of guys? Yeah, I read interesting shit online or
read people's books, then I'll send the publicist a message: hey, see if this guy is willing to do it. But when it comes to comedy, you just call them, right?

Yeah, yeah. Comics, I just call them. We have this problem — I don't know if you have it — where everyone we want on our show doesn't want to be on it, and tons of people we don't want on want to be on it.

Oh, that's a problem. Anybody who wants to be on that you don't want on, you've got to be stern with that. I've fucked that up a few times, where I had people on I didn't really want, and I was like, oh, what a douchey

fucking conversation that was. There have been a few of those. [nervous] Please don't tell us it was us. So wait, your advice is — take them or don't take them? Don't take the people you don't want on. Ever. Just gotta be able to say, ah, I'm not feeling it. No, just don't do it.

You know what you're doing, you know what you like, you know what you don't like. Just stick with it. When people are chasing after you to get on your podcast, most of the time they're not people you'd be chasing after. It's an unnatural situation.
